subject: sociology
chapter_title: Terms, Concepts and Their Use in Sociology

concepts.title: Social Groups: Aggregate, Category and Quasi-Group
concepts.definition: A social group exists only where people interact regularly, share a sense of belonging and define themselves as members. Mere gatherings and mere collections of similar people are not groups: an aggregate is people physically together (a bus queue), a category is people alike in some trait (all tall persons), and a quasi-group has common interests but no organisation yet.
concepts.key_idea: Interaction plus membership feeling makes a group -- not proximity, not similarity alone.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy102.txt lines 15-140 (social group and society, aggregate, category, quasi group, examples of crowd and audience)
question_patterns: define a social group and distinguish it from an aggregate and a category
in class 11 terms and concepts in sociology: what is a quasi group
is a crowd watching a cricket match a social group
why does a category of similar people not form a group
give examples of aggregate category and group from daily life
how does a quasi group turn into a group

solution_steps.explain: Ask whether members interact recurrently and feel 'we-ness'; that is the group test.
People merely present together form an aggregate; people merely alike form a category; people with shared interests but no structure form a quasi-group.
A quasi-group acquires organisation and identity -- say a trade union -- and becomes a genuine group.

worked_examples.q: People physically together, like a bus queue, form an aggregate or a group?

concepts.title: Status and Role: Ascribed and Achieved
concepts.definition: Status is a person's position in a social system, carrying honour or rank; role is the behaviour expected of whoever occupies that status. Some statuses are ascribed at birth -- caste, sex, royal birth -- while achieved statuses are earned through effort, and each person holds a whole cluster of statuses at once.
concepts.key_idea: You occupy a status and perform its role -- some statuses are given at birth, others are earned.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy102.txt lines 140-260 (status and role, ascribed and achieved status, role conflict, multiple statuses, role set)
question_patterns: distinguish status from role with examples
in class 11 terms and concepts in sociology: what are ascribed and achieved statuses
explain role conflict with a concrete example
why does one person hold many statuses at the same time
is the status of daughter in law ascribed or achieved
how do roles attached to a status guide behaviour

solution_steps.explain: Status is where one stands in the system of positions; role is the expected conduct that goes with the position.
Ascribed statuses come unbidden at birth; achieved statuses are won by individual action.
Multiple statuses can pull one person in opposite directions -- the teacher who must fail her own child faces role conflict.

worked_examples.q: Caste is an ascribed or an achieved status?

concepts.title: Social Control, Society and Community
concepts.definition: Society is the largest web of relationships marked by self-sufficiency and continuity, while a community is a smaller grouping held by locality and a feeling of belonging. Neither survives by goodwill alone: norms backed by sanctions -- folkways, mores and laws -- exert social control, rewarding conformity and punishing deviation.
concepts.key_idea: Norms are the traffic rules of social life -- sanctions, soft or hard, keep everyone on the road.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy102.txt lines 260-380 (society and community, social control, norms folkways mores and laws, sanctions)
question_patterns: distinguish society from community in sociology
in class 11 terms and concepts in sociology: explain folkways mores and laws as instruments of social control
how do sanctions enforce norms
give an example of a folkway and a more in indian society
why is social control necessary for group life
compare informal and formal social control

solution_steps.explain: Community implies locality and belonging; society is the wider, more abstract network of relationships.
Folkways are everyday usages, mores carry moral weight, laws are formalised and state-enforced.
Sanctions -- ridicule, ostracism, fine, imprisonment -- keep conduct within normative bounds without any central director.

worked_examples.q: Norms backed by sanctions exert what?

concepts.title: Culture: Nature versus Nurture
concepts.definition: Culture is the learned, shared design of living -- beliefs, values, practices and artefacts -- that distinguishes human groups. The nature versus nurture debate asks how much of behaviour is biological instinct and how much cultural learning; sociology stresses nurture, showing how the same biological needs are satisfied in strikingly different ways across cultures.
concepts.key_idea: Humans are born unfinished -- culture completes us, teaching what nature never specified.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy102.txt lines 380-460 (nature versus nurture debate, culture as learned behaviour, instinct and socialisation preview)
question_patterns: explain the nature versus nurture debate in sociology
in class 11 terms and concepts in sociology: why is culture called learned behaviour
show with an example how the same need is met differently across cultures
what does it mean to say humans lack instincts
how does culture make human life possible
distinguish cultural behaviour from instinctive behaviour

solution_steps.explain: Humans share bodily needs -- food, sex, shelter -- with other animals.
How those needs are met -- what counts as food, marriage or home -- varies enormously and must be learned.
Because the content is learned and shared, it is culture, and socialisation transmits it to each generation.

worked_examples.q: Is culture learned or inherited biologically?

worked_examples.question_pattern: A woman is a doctor, a mother, a Municipal councillor and a Gujarati. Identify her statuses and discuss which are ascribed or achieved, then point out a possible role conflict.

solution_template.explain: Doctor, mother, councillor and Gujarati are positions she occupies simultaneously -- a status set.
Motherhood-by-birth community ties are ascribed; doctor and councillor are achieved through training and election.
A night emergency in the hospital may clash with council duties -- the same person pulled by two roles.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Someone eats with the left hand at a ritual dinner, gossips about a neighbour, and later evades income tax. Classify each act against folkways, mores and laws with suitable sanctions.

solution_template.explain: Eating with the 'wrong' hand breaches a folkway; the sanction is mild -- comment or amusement.
Malicious gossip violates mores, inviting moral censure and social distance.
Tax evasion breaks law, inviting formal punishment -- showing how norms escalate from usage to morality to legality.
